claims.plain: Distal dendritic inhibition cuts firing the same way perisomatic inhibition does, by raising the spike threshold rather than by suppressing dendritic spikes.
Perisomatic and distal inhibition work through one shared mechanism, so perisomatic inhibition also controls dendritic spiking.
Phase-dependent control of dendritic spikes and spike timing needs many cycles of a rhythm to build up.
Beta-rhythm inhibition on distal dendrites both raises dendritic spiking in its troughs and suppresses it in its peaks.
Clustered apical inputs reach the soma when they arrive in the trough of a distal beta rhythm and are blocked at its peak.
Across a sweep of rhythm frequencies, beta near 20 Hz locks distal dendritic Ca²⁺ and NMDA spikes to phase most strongly.
Phase-dependent control of dendritic spikes and spike timing appears within the first few cycles of a beta or gamma burst.
Ca²⁺ spikes in apical tuft dendrites lead somatic action potentials by about 20 ms, most tightly in the most distal compartments.
Doubling distal dendritic inhibition nearly silences the neuron by shutting down dendritic Ca²⁺ and NMDA spikes, not by raising spike threshold.
Changing the delay between excitation and inhibition barely moves the firing rate but changes which dendrites drive the spikes.
Gamma-rhythm inhibition near the soma gates clustered proximal and basal inputs by phase while leaving distal apical inputs largely alone.
Across a sweep of rhythm frequencies, gamma modulates the somatic spike threshold most strongly when inhibition sits near the soma.
Gamma rhythms near the soma shift the spike threshold by phase without changing how often dendritic spikes occur.
Perisomatic inhibition controls the soma's spike output, while distal dendritic inhibition controls dendritic spikes and their timing.
A rhythm controls a compartment best when its cycle matches the local spike timescale — gamma at the soma, beta at distal dendrites.
Earlier work found that PV+ interneurons target the soma and accompany gamma, while SST+ interneurons target distal dendrites and beta.
Every result comes from a compartmental model of one layer 5 pyramidal neuron, with no network or population effects simulated.
Na+ dendritic spikes in proximal compartments lead somatic action potentials by 2–3 ms, with coupling weakening farther from the soma.
Synaptic drive uses published experimental parameters and yields a typical in vivo firing rate, with no sensitivity analysis over those choices.
NMDA spikes lead somatic action potentials by about 25 ms, longer than Na+ spikes because their kinetics are slower.
Doubling perisomatic inhibition nearly silences the neuron by raising the spike threshold, while dendritic spikes carry on.
Perisomatic inhibition lowers both the neuron's baseline firing and the slope of its input-output curve, compressing its dynamic range.
Distal inhibition should work best at beta, whose cycle matches the roughly 20–25 ms lead of dendritic spikes over somatic spikes.
Doubling distal dendritic inhibition should cut firing by suppressing apical Ca²⁺ and NMDA spikes, leaving the spike threshold alone.
Perisomatic inhibition should work best at gamma, whose cycles match the 2–3 ms lead of proximal Na+ spikes over somatic spikes.
Beta at the distal dendrites should gate apical inputs and gamma at the soma should gate basal inputs, each working independently.
Perisomatic inhibition should both shift and flatten the somatic input-output curve rather than simply moving its operating point.
Doubling perisomatic inhibition should cut firing by raising the somatic spike threshold, leaving dendritic Ca²⁺ and NMDA spikes intact.
The model explains why PV+ cells pair with gamma and SST+ cells with beta: each rhythm is optimal where that cell type makes its synapses.
